title: Prototypes & Inheritance
tagline: The object model under the hood: chains, new, classes as sugar, and when to compose instead of inherit.

lessons.title: The Prototype Chain: __proto__ vs prototype
lessons.body:
# The Prototype Chain: `__proto__` vs `prototype`

Every JavaScript object carries a hidden link to another object — its **prototype**. When you read a property the object doesn't have itself, the engine follows that link and keeps looking up the chain. That walk *is* inheritance in JavaScript. There is no class table consulted at compile time; the chain is per-object, resolved at runtime, and mutable.

## `__proto__` and `prototype` are different things

This is the single most-tested distinction in the topic, so nail it:

- **`obj.__proto__`** (spec name: `[[Prototype]]`) — the actual link *from an object* to its parent. `__proto__` itself is just a legacy accessor sitting on `Object.prototype`; the modern API is `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`.
- **`Fn.prototype`** — a property that exists *on functions*. It points to the object that will become the `[[Prototype]]` of instances created with `new Fn()`. Plain objects don't have a meaningful `.prototype`.

```js
function Dog(name) { this.name = name; }

const d = new Dog('Rex');
Object.getPrototypeOf(d) === Dog.prototype;   // true — d's link points at Dog.prototype
d.__proto__ === Dog.prototype;                // true — same link, legacy accessor
Dog.prototype.__proto__ === Object.prototype; // true — the chain continues
Object.prototype.__proto__ === null;          // true — the chain ends
```

## Property lookup walks the chain; assignment doesn't

Reading `d.trick` checks `d` itself, then `Dog.prototype`, then `Object.prototype`, then gives up with `undefined`. Two consequences interviewers love:

1. **The link is live, not a copy.** Mutating `Dog.prototype` after instances exist changes what every instance sees.
2. **Assignment shadows.** `d.trick = 'roll over'` creates an *own* property on `d`. It never writes through to the prototype.

```js
Dog.prototype.species = 'canine';
const d2 = new Dog('Max');
d2.species; // 'canine' — found on the prototype

d2.species = 'good boy'; // shadows: own property on d2, prototype untouched
d.species;               // still 'canine'
delete d2.species;
d2.species; // 'canine' again — the shadow is gone
```

## The full chain for everyday values

```js
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
Object.getPrototypeOf(arr) === Array.prototype;              // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype; // true

const fn = () => {};
Object.getPrototypeOf(fn) === Function.prototype; // true
```

Arrays get `map`/`filter` from `Array.prototype` and `hasOwnProperty` from `Object.prototype` — one continuous chain. `Object.create(null)` builds an object whose chain is empty (no `toString`, no `hasOwnProperty`): the standard trick for safe dictionary objects where user keys must never collide with inherited members.
lessons.comparisonNote: In Java, the inheritance chain belongs to the *class* and is fixed at compile time — method dispatch walks superclasses, but the hierarchy itself never changes at runtime. In JavaScript the chain belongs to each *object*, is resolved dynamically, and is mutable: `Object.setPrototypeOf` can rewire an object's parent after creation, something Java has no equivalent for. Mental model shift: Java's hierarchy is a blueprint drawn once; JS's is a parent pointer carried by every object.
keyPoints: `__proto__` is the link from an object to its parent; `prototype` is the template object a function stamps onto its instances.
Property reads walk the chain to `null`; property writes create shadowing own properties — they never mutate the prototype.
Prototype links are live: mutating a prototype object is immediately visible to all instances.

lessons.title: new: The Four-Step Algorithm
lessons.comparisonNote: In Java, `new` is a JVM-level operation: it always allocates the object and runs the constructor — there is no way to intercept or redefine what `new` does. In JavaScript, `new` is just the four-step algorithm above, which is why you can polyfill it by hand. The other shock for Java developers: a JS 'constructor' is an *ordinary function*. Its only constructor-ish power is the `.prototype` property from the previous lesson. Java ties constructors to the class name; JS ties construction behavior to a property on a function.
keyPoints: `new` = fresh object → link `[[Prototype]]` to `Fn.prototype` → call with `this` → object return wins, otherwise the fresh object.
A constructor returning an object discards the new instance; returning a primitive is ignored.
Calling a constructor function without `new` runs it as a plain function — `this` is global (sloppy) or `undefined` (strict).
`new.target` detects new-less calls; `class` constructors throw when called without `new`.

lessons.title: class Is Sugar: Desugaring, Statics, extends/super
lessons.comparisonNote: Two shocks for Java developers. First, Java statics are *hidden*, not inherited — a subclass doesn't polymorphically inherit static methods, and there is no 'static chain.' In JS, link #2 above (`Corgi.__proto__ === Dog`) means static methods genuinely inherit down the constructor chain, and `super` works inside static methods too. Second, Java classes are nominal types enforced by the compiler; JS classes are syntax sugar over the same mutable prototype links from lesson 1 — `extends` just automates the `Object.setPrototypeOf` calls you could write by hand.
keyPoints: `class` desugars to a constructor function plus prototype assignments; methods are non-enumerable and classes aren't hoisted.
In a derived constructor, `super()` must run before `this` is touched — the parent call is what creates `this`.
`super.method()` is sugar for a method lookup on the parent prototype.

lessons.title: instanceof, Object.create, and Composition over Inheritance
lessons.comparisonNote: Java nudges you toward `extends` as the default reuse mechanism (though *Effective Java* Item 18 — 'favor composition over inheritance' — is the most-quoted counterpoint). In JavaScript the advice is stronger, for a mechanical reason: the chain is mutable and shared. Anyone can mutate `Parent.prototype` at runtime and change every descendant's behavior, so deep hierarchies are fragile in a way Java's compile-time-fixed hierarchies are not. And where Java's `instanceof` checks a nominal type lattice the compiler guarantees, JS's `instanceof` checks one rewirable link — it can lie, which is why production code often prefers duck-typing or `Symbol` brand checks.
keyPoints: `instanceof` only asks whether `Ctor.prototype` is in the object's chain — reassigning prototypes or crossing realms breaks it.
`Object.create(proto)` is inheritance with no constructor; `Object.create(null)` gives prototype-free dictionary objects.
Prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a): assemble behavior from small units instead of growing taxonomies.
React already chose composition — hooks and HOCs over class hierarchies.

exercises.title: Predict the chain lookups
exercises.prompt:
Predict what each `console.log` prints, then run the solution to check yourself. For each line, be able to say *where* in the chain the value was found (or why it wasn't).

```js
const base = { a: 1, b: 2 };
const mid = Object.create(base);
mid.b = 20;
const leaf = Object.create(mid);

console.log('Q1:', leaf.a); // ?
console.log('Q2:', leaf.b); // ?
console.log('Q3:', leaf.c); // ?
mid.a = 100;
console.log('Q4:', leaf.a); // ?
console.log('Q5:', leaf.hasOwnProperty('b'), 'b' in leaf); // ?
```

Expected solution output:
```
Q1: 1 — inherited from base through mid
Q2: 20 — mid's own property shadows base.b
Q3: undefined — nowhere in the chain
Q4: 100 — the link is live, not a copy; mutating base is visible via leaf
Q5: false true — 'b' is not an own property of leaf, but is found via the chain
```
hints: Read `leaf.a` by walking: does `leaf` have its own `a`? Does `mid`? Does `base`?
`mid.b = 20` creates an *own* property on `mid` — it doesn't touch `base.b`. What does that mean for `leaf.b`?
For Q5, remember the difference: `hasOwnProperty` checks only the object itself, `in` walks the whole chain.

exercises.title: Polyfill new
exercises.prompt:
Implement `myNew(Constructor, ...args)` replicating the four-step `new` algorithm from the lesson: fresh object, link `[[Prototype]]` to `Constructor.prototype`, call with `this`, and let an object return value win.

```js
function Person(name) { this.name = name; }
Person.prototype.greet = function () { return `hi, ${this.name}`; };

const p = myNew(Person, 'Ray');
console.log(p.name);              // 'Ray'
console.log(p.greet());           // 'hi, Ray'
console.log(p instanceof Person); // true

function ReturnsObj() { this.x = 1; return { y: 2 }; }
const ro = myNew(ReturnsObj);
console.log(ro.y, ro.x);          // 2 undefined

function ReturnsPrim() { this.x = 1; return 42; }
console.log(myNew(ReturnsPrim).x); // 1
```

Expected solution output:
```
Ray
hi, Ray
true
2 undefined
1
```
hints: `Object.create(Constructor.prototype)` does steps 1 and 2 in a single call.
Step 3 is just `Constructor.apply(obj, args)` — capture its return value for step 4.
Step 4's check: `typeof result === 'object'` needs a `null` guard, and functions count as objects too.

exercises.title: Implement instanceof
exercises.prompt:
Implement `myInstanceof(obj, Ctor)` that walks `obj`'s prototype chain looking for `Ctor.prototype`. Verify it against the native operator on every case below — each line prints your result vs native, and the final line must be `all match: true`.

```js
class A {}
class B extends A {}
const b = new B();
const dict = Object.create(null);

check(b, B);      // my=true native=true
check(b, A);      // my=true native=true
check(b, Object); // my=true native=true
check(b, Array);  // my=false native=false
check(5, Number); // my=false native=false (primitives have no chain)
check(dict, Object); // my=false native=false (null-prototype object)
```

Expected solution output:
```
b instanceof B: my=true native=true
b instanceof A: my=true native=true
b instanceof Object: my=true native=true
b instanceof Array: my=false native=false
5 instanceof Number: my=false native=false
dict instanceof Object: my=false native=false
all match: true
```
hints: Guard the top: `null`, `undefined`, and primitives return `false` without touching the chain (native `instanceof` never throws on the left side).
The loop is: `proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`, compare with `Ctor.prototype`, advance until `null`.
Functions are valid left-hand operands (`typeof fn === 'function'` has a chain), so don't exclude them.

exercises.title: Refactor a hierarchy to composition
hints: Define each behavior once as a method on a shared unit object — then `mgr.work === eng.work` is `true` because it's literally the same function reference.
`Object.assign({ name, pay, teamSize }, canWork, hasPay, canManage)` gives a flat object: data plus composed behaviors, prototype still `Object.prototype`.
Methods use `this`, so they must be called as `mgr.work()` — detached references (`const w = mgr.work; w()`) lose the binding, same as in the class version.
